lead: Ephesians calls the sleeper to rise from the dead so that Christ may shine on him, and then describes a community filled with the Spirit, singing and giving thanks to the Father at all times. Mark shows a crowd in a deserted place at evening, and Jesus who takes five loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks and gives. Both readings end at a table of thanksgiving, the table the Church sets in every Holy Qurbana. The key words are light, thanksgiving and broken bread.

set: The second half of Ephesians turns from God's plan in Christ to the life that follows from it. Just before this passage the letter contrasts the works of darkness with life as “children of light” (5:8). Ephesians presents itself as Paul's; many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name, while others hold that it is Paul's own.

Verse 14 introduces a quotation with “Therefore it says”, but the words are not found in the Old Testament. Many scholars think they come from an early Christian hymn sung at baptism, when the newly baptized came up from the water into the light.
str: vv. 13–14: what the light exposes becomes light; the baptismal call to rise.
vv. 15–17: live wisely; make the most of the time.
v. 18: not drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit.
vv. 19–21: psalms and hymns, thanksgiving at all times, mutual submission.
kw: The verb is used of the dawn. Christ comes on the sleeper as the sun rises on the world. The early Church called baptism “enlightenment” (compare Hebrews 6:4).
making the most of the time
Literally “buying up the opportune moment”, as a merchant buys up goods while they are available. Each day holds chances for good that will not come again.
A command in the present tense: keep on being filled. Being filled with the Spirit is not a single event but a way of life.
vv: Sleeper, awake! Rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.

Clement of Alexandria knew a longer form of this hymn, which goes on to speak of Christ as the Sun of the Resurrection (in substance). In the season of the Resurrection we hear it as our own baptismal call.
Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery; but be filled with the Spirit,
At Pentecost some onlookers thought the apostles were drunk (Acts 2:13). The Spirit gives a joy that does not come from a cup.
giving thanks to God the Father at all times and for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The Greek verb is eucharisteō, from which the word Eucharist comes.
ch: The Church's sung liturgy takes up this passage: psalms, hymns and spiritual songs addressed to the Father through Christ in the Spirit. The Catechism teaches that singing and music serve the liturgy when they express prayer, unite the assembly and give solemnity to the celebration (CCC 1157). Thanksgiving “at all times and for everything” is the spirit of the Holy Qurbana, the great thanksgiving of the Church. Verse 21 opens the passage on Christian households that follows; all its instructions stand under mutual reverence for Christ.

set: The apostles have returned from their first mission, and Jesus has taken them to a deserted place to rest. A great crowd follows, and he has compassion on them, “because they were like sheep without a shepherd” (6:34), recalling Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34. He teaches them, and now it is late.
Apart from the Resurrection, this is the only miracle of Jesus told in all four Gospels. John adds that the Passover was near (John 6:4), which fits Mark's “green grass” of spring.
str: vv. 35–36: the disciples' practical advice: send them away.
vv. 37–38: “You give them something to eat”; five loaves and two fish.
vv. 39–40: the crowd seated in groups on the green grass.
v. 41: the blessing and the breaking.
vv. 42–44: all are filled; twelve baskets; five thousand men.
kw: The wilderness recalls Israel fed with manna (Exodus 16). God feeds his people where nothing grows.
The Jewish blessing over bread praises God who brings forth bread from the earth. Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives, the same four actions as at the Last Supper (Mark 14:22).
The word for the fragments. The Didache, a very early Christian writing, uses the same word for the bread broken at the Eucharist (Didache 9).
vv: You give them something to eat.
The disciples see a problem to send away; Jesus sees people to feed, and he makes his disciples part of the answer.
Then he ordered them to get all the people to sit down in groups on the green grass.
Mark says literally “table-groups, table-groups”. Many hear Psalm 23 here: the shepherd makes his flock lie down in green pastures and spreads a table.
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, and blessed and broke the loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people;
He gives through the disciples. The Lord still feeds his people through the hands of those he sends.
and they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish.
Twelve, the number of the tribes of Israel and of the apostles. There is more than enough.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord says the blessing, breaks and distributes the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigures the superabundance of the one bread of his Eucharist (CCC 1335). The Holy Qurbana is this table: the Lord's compassion for the hungry, his blessing to the Father, his body broken and given through the hands of his ministers. And the command “You give them something to eat” sends the Church to the hungry of the world.

qa: Was the multiplication a real miracle, or only the crowd sharing what they had brought?

All four Gospels present it as a miracle worked by Jesus, and the Church reads it so. The idea that the crowd simply shared their food is a modern explanation that the texts do not support. The sign is real, and it points beyond itself to the Bread of Life.
study: Where is the Lord saying to me, “You give them something to eat”?
Ephesians asks for thanks “at all times and for everything”. For what do I find it hardest to give thanks?
